entries.c775d2e2b608712a3380e9a7125411dc247b0c33: <div sID="gen8192" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="2Chr.17" sID="2Chr.17"/> <div eID="gen8192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8193" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8194" type="x-p"/> Here begin the life and reign of Jehoshaphat, who was one of the first three among the royal worthies, one of the best that ever swayed the sceptre of Judah since David's head was laid. He was the good son of a good father, so that, as this time, grace ran in the blood, even in the blood-royal. Happy the son that had such a father, to lay a good foundation in him and for him. Happy the father that had such a son, to build so wall upon the foundation he had laid! Happy the kingdom that was blessed with two such kings, two such reigns, together! In this chapter we have, I. His accession to and establishment in the throne, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1-2Chr.17.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">5</reference>. II. His personal piety, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.3-2Chr.17.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">6</reference>. III. The course he took to promote religion in his kingdom, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7-2Chr.17.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. IV. The mighty sway he bore among the neighbours, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10-2Chr.17.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. V. The great strength of his kingdom, both in garrisons and standing forces, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12-2Chr.17.19">ver. 12-19</reference>. Thus was his prosperity the reward of his piety and his piety the brightest grace and ornament of his prosperity.
entries.2931a48854eee4e8802be7f6ed042d8e7e6b23a7: <div eID="gen8194" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8193" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoshaphat Succeeds Asa. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 914.)</title> <div sID="gen8195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead, and strengthened himself against Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he placed forces in all the fenced cities of Judah, and set garrisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim, which Asa his father had taken. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the first ways of his father David, and sought not unto Baalim; <hi type="super">4</hi> But sought to the <hi type="italic"><hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> </hi> God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stablished the kingdom in his hand; and all Judah brought to Jehoshaphat presents; and he had riches and honour in abundance. <hi type="super">6</hi> And his heart was lifted up in the ways of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : moreover he took away the high places and groves out of Judah. <hi type="super">7</hi> Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to Ben-hail, and to Obadiah, and to Zechariah, and to Nethaneel, and to Michaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah. <hi type="super">8</hi> And with them <hi type="italic">he sent</hi> Levites, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they taught in Judah, and <hi type="italic">had</hi> the book of the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people. <div eID="gen8195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8196" type="x-p"/> Here we find concerning Jehoshaphat, <div eID="gen8196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8197" type="x-p"/> I. What a wise man he was. As soon as he came to the crown he <hi type="italic">strengthened himself against Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1">v. 1</reference>. Ahab, an active warlike prince, had now been three years upon the throne of Israel, the vigour of his beginning falling in with the decay of Asa's conclusion. It is probable that the kingdom of Israel had, of late, got ground of the kingdom of Judah and began to grow formidable to it; so that the first thing Jehoshaphat had to do was to make his part good on that side, and to check the growing greatness of the king of Israel, which he did so effectually, and without bloodshed, that Ahab soon courted his alliance, so far was he from giving him any disturbance, and proved more dangerous as a friend than he could have been as an enemy. Jehoshaphat strengthened himself not to act offensively against Israel or invade them, but only to maintain his own, which he did by fortifying the cities that were on his frontiers, and putting garrisons, stronger than had been, in the cities of Ephraim, which he was master of, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.2">v. 2</reference>. He did not strengthen himself, as his father did, by a league with the king of Syria, but by fair and regular methods, on which he might expect the blessing of God and in which he trusted God. <div eID="gen8197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8198" type="x-p"/> II. What a good man he was. It is an excellent character that is here given him. 1. He <hi type="italic">walked in the ways of his father David.</hi> In the characters of the kings, David's ways are often made the standard, as <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.3">1 Kings xv. 3, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.11">2 Kings xiv. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.3">xvi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.3">xviii. 3</reference>. But the distinction is nowhere so strongly marked as here between his first ways and his last ways; for the last were not so good as the first. His ways, before he fell so foully in the matter of Uriah (which is mentioned long afterwards as the bar in his escutcheon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.5">1 Kings xv. 5</reference>), were good ways, and, though he happily recovered from that fall, yet perhaps he never, while he lived, fully retrieved the spiritual strength and comfort he lost by it. Jehoshaphat followed David as far as he followed God and no further. Paul himself thus limits our imitation of him (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1 Cor. xi. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Follow me, as I follow Christ,</hi> and not otherwise. Many good people have had their first ways, which were their best ways, their first love, which was their strongest love; and in every copy we propose to write after, as we must single out that only which is good, so that chiefly which is best. The words here will admit another reading; they run thus: <hi type="italic">He walked in the ways of David his father (Hareshonim), those first ways,</hi> or those <hi type="italic">ancient ways.</hi> He proposed to himself, for his example, the primitive times of the royal family, those purest times, before the corruptions of the late reigns came in. See <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>. The LXX. leaves out David, and so refers it to Asa: <hi type="italic">He walked in the first ways of his father,</hi> and did not imitate him in what was amiss in him, towards the latter end of his time. It is good to be cautious in following the best men, lest we step aside after them. 2. He <hi type="italic">sought not to Baalim, but sought to the Lord God of his father,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.3-2Chr.17.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The neighbouring nations had their Baalim, one had one Baal and another had another; but he abhorred them all, had nothing to do with them. He <hi type="italic">worshipped the Lord God of his father</hi> and him only, prayed to him only and enquired of him only; both are included in seeking him. 3. That he <hi type="italic">walked in God's commandments,</hi> not only worshipped the true God, but worshipped him according to his own institution, <hi type="italic">and not after the doings of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.4">v. 4</reference>. Though the king of Israel was his neighbour and ally, yet he did not learn his way. Whatever dealings he had with him in civil matters, he would not have communion with him, nor comply with him in his religion. In this he kept close to the rule. 4. <hi type="italic">His heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">v. 6</reference>), or <hi type="italic">he lifted up his heart.</hi> He brought his heart to his work, and lifted up his heart in it; that is, he had a sincere regard to God in it. <hi type="italic">Unto thee, O Lord! do I lift up my soul.</hi> His heart was enlarged in that which is good, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Ps. cxix. 32</reference>. He never thought he could do enough for God. He was lively and affectionate in his religion, <hi type="italic">fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,</hi> cheerful and pleasant in it; he went on in his work with alacrity, as Jacob, who, after his vision of God at Bethel, <hi type="italic">lifted up his feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1">Gen. xxix. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">margin.</hi> He was bold and resolute in the ways of God and went on with courage. His heart was lifted up above the consideration of the difficulties that were in the way of his duty; he easily got over them all, and was not frightened with <hi type="italic">winds and clouds</hi> from <hi type="italic">sowing and reaping,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>. Let us walk in the same spirit. <div eID="gen8198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8199" type="x-p"/> III. What a useful man he was, not only a good man, but a good king. He not only was good himself, but did good in his generation, did a great deal of good. 1. He took away the teachers of lies, so images are called (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">Hab. ii. 18</reference>), the <hi type="italic">high places</hi> and <hi type="italic">the groves,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">v. 6</reference>. It is meant of those in which idols were worshipped; for those that were dedicated to the true God only were not taken away, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.33">ch. xx. 33</reference>. It was only idolatry that he abolished. Nothing debauched the nation more than those idolatrous groves or images which he took away. 2. He sent forth teachers of truth. When he enquired into the state of religion in his kingdom he found his people generally very ignorant: they <hi type="italic">knew not that they did evil.</hi> Even in the last good reign there had been little care taken to instruct them in their duty; and therefore Jehoshaphat resolves to begin his work at the right end, deals with them as reasonable creatures, will not lead them blindfold, no, not into a reformation, but endeavours to have them well taught, knowing that that was the way to have them well cured. In this good work he employed, (1.) His princes. Those about him he sent forth; those in the country he sent <hi type="italic">to teach in the cities of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7">v. 7</reference>. He ordered them, in the administration of justice, not only to correct the people when they did ill, but to teach them how to do better, and to give a reason for what they did, that the people might be informed of the difference between good and evil. The princes or judges upon the bench have a great opportunity of teaching people their duty to God and man, and it is not out of their province, for the laws of God are to be looked upon as laws of the land. (2.) The <hi type="italic">Levites</hi> and <hi type="italic">priests</hi> went <hi type="italic">with the princes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">taught in Judah, having the book of the law with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.8-2Chr.17.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. They were teachers by office, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.10">Deut. xxxiii. 10</reference>. Teaching was part of the work for which they had their maintenance. The priests and the Levites had little else to do. But, it seems, they had neglected it, pretending perhaps that they could not get the people to hear them. "Well," says Jehoshaphat, "you shall go along with the princes, and they with their authority shall oblige the people to come and hear you; and then, if they be not well instructed, it is your fault." What an abundance of good may be done when Moses and Aaron thus go hand in hand in the doing of it, when princes with their power, and priests and Levites with their scripture learning, agree to teach the people the good knowledge of God and their duty! These itinerant judges and itinerant preachers together were instrumental to diffuse a blessed light throughout the cities of Judah. But it is said, <hi type="italic">They had the book of the law of the Lord with them.</hi> [1.] For their own direction, that thence they might fetch all the instructions they gave to the people, and not <hi type="italic">teach for doctrines the commandments of men.</hi> [2.] For the conviction of the people, that they might see that they had a divine warrant for what they said and delivered to them that only which they received from the Lord. Note, Ministers, when they go to teach the people, should have their Bibles with them. <div eID="gen8199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8200" type="x-p"/> IV. What a happy man he was. 1. How happy he was in the favour of his God, who signally owned and blessed him: <hi type="italic">The Lord was with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.3">v. 3</reference>); <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord was his helper</hi> (so the Chaldee paraphrase); <hi type="italic">the Lord established the kingdom in his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">v. 5</reference>. Those stand firmly that have the presence of God with them. If the <hi type="italic">beauty of the Lord our God be upon us,</hi> that will <hi type="italic">establish the work of our hands</hi> and establish us in our integrity. 2. How happy he was in the affections of his people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">All Judah brought him presents,</hi> in acknowledgment of his kindness in sending preachers among them. The more there is of true religion among a people the more there will be of conscientious loyalty. A government that answers the end of government will be supported. The effect of the favour both of God and his kingdom was that he had <hi type="italic">riches and honour in abundance.</hi> It is undoubtedly true, though few will believe it, that religion and piety are the best friends to outward prosperity. And, observe, it follows immediately, <hi type="italic">His heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord.</hi> Riches and honour in abundance prove to many a clog and a hindrance in the ways of the Lord, an occasion of pride, security, and sensuality; but they had a quite contrary effect upon Jehoshaphat: his abundance was oil to the wheels of his obedience, and the more he had of the wealth of this world the more was his heart <hi type="italic">lifted up in the ways of the Lord.</hi>
entries.8af44d8999dff89ddd1da167ed6d8d0193f8fda1: <div eID="gen8200" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoshaphat's Prosperity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 911.)</title> <div sID="gen8201" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that <hi type="italic">were</hi> round about Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat. <hi type="super">11</hi> Also <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents, and tribute silver; and the Arabians brought him flocks, seven thousand and seven hundred rams, and seven thousand and seven hundred he goats. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Jehoshaphat waxed great exceedingly; and he built in Judah castles, and cities of store. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he had much business in the cities of Judah: and the men of war, mighty men of valour, <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">14</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the numbers of them according to the house of their fathers: Of Judah, the captains of thousands; Adnah the chief, and with him mighty men of valour three hundred thousand. <hi type="super">15</hi> And next to him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Jehohanan the captain, and with him two hundred and fourscore thousand. <hi type="super">16</hi> And next him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Amasiah the son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and with him two hundred thousand mighty men of valour. <hi type="super">17</hi> And of Benjamin; Eliada a mighty man of valour, and with him armed men with bow and shield two hundred thousand. <hi type="super">18</hi> And next him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Jehozabad, and with him a hundred and fourscore thousand ready prepared for the war. <hi type="super">19</hi> These waited on the king, beside <hi type="italic">those</hi> whom the king put in the fenced cities throughout all Judah. <div eID="gen8201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8202" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of Jehoshaphat's great prosperity and the flourishing state of his kingdom. <div eID="gen8202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8203" type="x-p"/> I. He had good interest in the neighbouring princes and nations. Though he was not perhaps so great a soldier as David (which might have made him their terror), nor so great a scholar as Solomon (which might have made him their oracle), yet <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord fell so upon them</hi> (that is, God so influenced and governed their spirits) that they had all a reverence for him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10">v. 10</reference>. And, 1. <hi type="italic">None of them made war against him.</hi> God's good providence so ordered it that, while the princes and priests were instructing and reforming the country, none of his neighbours gave him any molestations, to take him off from that good work. Thus when Jacob and his sons were going to worship at Bethel the terror of God was upon the neighbouring cities, that they <hi type="italic">did not pursue after them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen. xxxv. 5</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Exod.34.24">Exod. xxxiv. 24</reference>. 2. Many of them brought presents to him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.11">v. 11</reference>), to secure his friendship. Perhaps these were a tribute imposed upon them by Asa, who made himself master of the cities of the Philistines, and the tents of the Arabians, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14-2Chr.14.15">ch. xiv. 14, 15</reference>. With the 7700 rams, and the same number of he-goats, which the Arabians brought, there was probably a proportionable number of ewes and lambs, she-goats and kids. <div eID="gen8203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8204" type="x-p"/> II. He had a very considerable stores laid up in the cities of Judah. He pulled down his barns, and built larger (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">castles and cities of store,</hi> for arms and victuals. He was a man of business, and aimed at the public good in all his undertakings, either to preserve the peace or prepare for war. <div eID="gen8204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8205" type="x-p"/> III. He had the militia in good order. It was never in better since David modelled it. Five <hi type="italic">lord-lieutenants</hi> (if I may so call them) are here named, with the numbers of those under their command (the serviceable men, that were fit for war in their respective districts), three in Judah, and two in Benjamin. It is said of one of these great commanders, <hi type="italic">Amasiah,</hi> that <hi type="italic">he willingly offered himself unto the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.16">v. 16</reference>), not only to the king, to serve him in this post, but to the Lord, to glorify him in it. He was the most eminent among them for religion, he accepted the place, not for the honour, or power, or profit of it, but for conscience' sake towards God, that he might serve his country,. It was usual for great generals then to offer of their spoils to the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.26">1 Chron. xxvi. 26</reference>. But this good man offered himself first to the Lord, and then his dedicated things. The number of the soldiers under these five generals amounts to 1,160 000 men, a vast number for so small a compass of ground as Judah's and Benjamin's lot to furnish out and maintain. Abijah could bring into the field but 400,000 (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">ch. xiii. 3</reference>), Asa not 600,000 (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8">ch. xiv. 8</reference>), yet Jehoshaphat has at command almost 1,200 000. But it must be considered, 1. That God had promised to make the seed of Abraham like the sand of the sea for number. 2. There had now been a long peace. 3. We may suppose that the city of Jerusalem was very much enlarged. 4. Many had come over to them from the kingdom of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>), which would increase the numbers of the people. 5. Jehoshaphat was under a special blessing of God, which made his affairs to prosper greatly. The armies, we may suppose, were dispersed all the country over, and each man resided for the most part on his own estate; but they appeared often, to be mustered and trained, and were ready at call whenever there was occasion. The commanders waited on the king (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.19">v. 19</reference>) as officers of his court, privy-counsellors, and ministers of state. <div eID="gen8205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8206" type="x-p"/> But, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> observe, It was not this formidable army that struck a terror upon the neighbouring nations, that restrained them from attempting any thing against Israel, or obliged them to pay tribute, but the fear of God which fell upon them when Jehoshaphat reformed his country and set up a preaching ministry in it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10">v. 10</reference>. The ordinances of God are more the strength and safety of a kingdom than its military force—its men of God more than its men of war.  <chapter eID="2Chr.17"/> <div eID="gen8206" type="x-p"/>

entries.8604cc1e876e97058200bdd8e0bf73e6dac0e8bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4030"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <div sID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1-2Chr.17.6">2Ch 17:1-6</reference>. Jehoshaphat Reigns Well and Prospers.<div eID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4030"/><hi type="bold">1. Jehoshaphat ... strengthened himself against Israel--</hi>The temper and proceedings of the kings of Israel rendered it necessary for him to prepare vigorous measures of defense on the northern frontier of his kingdom. These consisted in filling all the fortresses with their full complement of troops and establishing military stations in various parts of the country, as well as in the cities of Mount Ephraim, which belonged to Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Ch 15:8</reference>). <div eID="gen5836" type="x-p"/>
entries.32b161241379dfcb6d3bd8cba4a46d5f32e4fc5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4031"/><div sID="gen5837" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4031"/><hi type="bold">3-5. he walked in the first ways of his father David--</hi>He imitated the piety of his great ancestor in the early part of his reign before he made those unhappy lapses which dishonored his character.<div eID="gen5837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and sought not unto Baalim--</hi>a term used for idols generally in contradistinction to the Lord God of his father. <div eID="gen5838" type="x-p"/>
entries.fee26199aafc9d101a64cfde6ffae231f43fc3fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4034"/><div sID="gen5841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4034"/><hi type="bold">6. his heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord--</hi>Full of faith and piety, he possessed zeal and courage to undertake the reformation of manners, to suppress all the works and objects of idolatry (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.33">2Ch 20:33</reference>), and he held out public encouragement to the pure worship of God.<div eID="gen5841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5842" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7-2Chr.17.11">2Ch 17:7-11</reference>. He Sends Levites to Teach in Judah. <div eID="gen5842" type="x-p"/>
entries.e086c323832b7f8024cd22535256d656b0555173: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4035"/><div sID="gen5843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4035"/><hi type="bold">7-11. Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes, ... to teach in the cities of Judah--</hi>The ordinary work of teaching devolved on the priests. But extraordinary commissioners were appointed, probably to ascertain whether the work had been done or neglected. This deputation of five princes, assisted by two priests and nine Levites, was to make a circuit of the towns in Judah. It is the first practical measure we read of as being adopted by any of the kings for the religious instruction of the people. Time and unbroken opportunities were afforded for carrying out fully this excellent plan of home education, for the kingdom enjoyed internal tranquillity as well as freedom for foreign wars. It is conformable to the pious style of the sacred historian to trace this profound peace to the "fear of the Lord having fallen on all kingdoms of the lands that were round about Judah." <div eID="gen5843" type="x-p"/>
entries.04e07468af16162193d9dd4b1486cfffbffb28c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4038"/><div sID="gen5848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4038"/><hi type="bold">14. these are the numbers--</hi>The warriors were arranged in the army according to their fathers houses. The army of Jehoshaphat, commanded by five great generals and consisting of five unequal divisions, comprised one million one hundred and sixty thousand men, without including those who garrisoned the fortresses. No monarch, since the time of Solomon, equalled Jehoshaphat in the extent of his revenue, in the strength of his fortifications, and in the number of his troops. <chapter eID="2Chr.17"/>

entries.5e88ee10c65a08cbecc967f5e275d0bce88afac8: <div eID="gen14299" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14300" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14301" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14301" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14300" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14302" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat succeeds his father Asa, and reigns piously, and is particularly blessed, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1-2Chr.17.6">2Chr 17:1-6</reference>. He establishes an itinerant ministry, for the instruction of the people, through all the cities of Judah, which produces the most beneficial effects, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7-2Chr.17.10">2Chr 17:7-10</reference>. The Philistines and Arabians bring him gifts, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.11">2Chr 17:11</reference>. His greatness, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12">2Chr 17:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.13">2Chr 17:13</reference>. The commanders of his troops, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.14-2Chr.17.19">2Chr 17:14-19</reference>. <div eID="gen14302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14303" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14304" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat - and strengthened himself against Israel - The kingdoms of Israel and Judah were rivals from the beginning; sometimes one, sometimes the other, prevailed. Asa and Baasha were nearly matched; but, after Baasha's death, Israel was greatly weakened by civil contentions, and Jehoshaphat got the ascendancy. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.16-1Kgs.16.23">1Kgs 16:16-23</reference>.
entries.b1b725bf65c3544c6c51b4f75da5bd982f77e3b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14305" type="x-p"/> The cities of Ephraim - This conquest from the kingdom of Israel is referred to, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Chr 15:8</reference>; but when it was made we do not know.
entries.39b9e0754b855c43fd57b3324520597f957fad37: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14306" type="x-p"/> The Lord was with Jehoshaphat - "The Word of the Lord was Jehoshaphat's Helper." - Targum.
entries.91892538c98e4b25f6d76850566c26b3f25e87f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14307" type="x-p"/> To teach in the cities of Judah - "To teach the fear of the Lord in the cities of Judah." - Targum. <div eID="gen14307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14308" type="x-p"/> In these verses we find a remarkable account of an itinerant ministry established by Jehoshaphat; and in this work he employed three classes of men: <div eID="gen14308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14309" type="x-p"/> 1. The princes. <div eID="gen14309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14310" type="x-p"/> 2. The Levites. <div eID="gen14310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14311" type="x-p"/> 3. The priests. <div eID="gen14311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> We may presume that the princes instructed the people in the nature of the civil law and constitution of the kingdom; the Levites instructed them in every thing that appertained to the temple service, and ritual law; and the priests instructed them in the nature and design of the religion they professed. Thus the nation became thoroughly instructed in their duty to God, to the king, and to each other. They became, therefore, as one man; and against a people thus united, on such principles, no enemy could be successful.
entries.8d9656874e43defa1ef69558fe1b821674336015: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14313" type="x-p"/> Had the book of the law of the Lord with them - This was their text book: it was the book of God; they taught it as such, and as such the people received it. Its laws were God's laws, and the people felt their obligation, and their consciences were bound. Thus they were obedient to the laws of the land, on the principle of religion. In this they were encouraged and confirmed by the example of all, both in Church and state. The princes were not only pious, but were teachers of piety; the Levites showed them the worth and excellence of their ritual institutions; and the priests showed them the moral use they were to make of the whole: and thus the people became obedient to God as well as to the king, and kept all the civil ordinances, not merely for the sake of a good king, but for the sake of a good and gracious God. By these means the nation enjoyed peace and prosperity; and all insurrections, seditions, and popular commotions, were prevented. The surrounding nations, perceiving this, saw that there was no hope of subduing such a people, so they made no war with Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10">2Chr 17:10</reference>. And they took care not to provoke such a people to fall on them; therefore, it is said, The fear of the Lord fell on all the kingdoms and lands that were round about Judah. Such an itinerant ministry established in these kingdoms for upwards of fourscore years, teaching the pure, unadulterated doctrines of the Gospel, with the propriety and necessity of obedience to the laws, has been the principal means, in the hand of God, of preserving these lands from those convulsions and revolutions that have ruined and nearly dissolved the European continent. The itinerant ministry, to which this refers, is that which was established in these lands by the late truly reverend, highly learned and cultivated, deeply pious and loyal John Wesley, A.M., formerly a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, whose followers are known by the name of Methodists; a people who are an honor to their country, and a blessing to the government under which they live.
entries.79c4a9b5dfcb34160e7efea41b6336778c7eea4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen14313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14314" type="x-p"/> The Philistines brought - presents - They and the Arabians purchased peace with the king of Judah by paying an annual tribute. The Philistines brought silver, and no doubt different kinds of merchandise, The Arabs, whose riches consisted in cattle, brought him flocks in great abundance, principally rams and he-goats.
entries.18dbeada45d6b94aa73ff185319b42d5c4638e09: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen14314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14315" type="x-p"/> He had much business in the cities - He kept the people constantly employed; they had wages for their work; and by their labors the empire was both enriched and strengthened.
entries.5615976de435912639c847e3d2b3d8ace447ed68: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14316" type="x-p"/> Adnah, the chief - He was generalissimo of all this host. These are the numbers of the five battalions: under Adnah, three hundred thousand; Jehohanan, two hundred and eighty thousand, Amasiah, two hundred thousand; Eliada, two hundred thousand; Jehozabad, one hundred and eighty thousand; in all, one million one hundred and sixty thousand.
entries.9b30ef9aa9075bfbaa1e05481cd2bfdfa5b496d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen14316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14317" type="x-p"/> These waited on the king - They were disposable forces, always at the king's command; and were independent of those by which the cities of Judah were garrisoned. <div eID="gen14317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14318" type="x-p"/> There is not a sovereign in Europe or in the world but might read this chapter with advantage. <div eID="gen14318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14319" type="x-p"/> 1. It shows most forcibly that true religion is the basis of the state, and that, wherever it prospers, there the state prospers. <div eID="gen14319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14320" type="x-p"/> 2. It shows also that it is the wisdom of kings to encourage religion with all their power and influence; for if the hearts of the subjects be not bound and influenced by true religion, vain is the application of laws, fines, imprisonments, or corporal punishment of any kind. <div eID="gen14320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14321" type="x-p"/> 3. A religious nation is ever a great nation; it is loved by its friends, it is dreaded by its enemies. <div eID="gen14321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14322" type="x-p"/> 4. It is ever a peaceable and united nation: the blessings of religion, and a wholesome and paternal government, are so fully felt and prized, that all find it their interest to preserve and defend them. Harmony, peace, piety, and strength, are the stability of such times. May Britain know and value them!  <chapter eID="2Chr.17"/> <div eID="gen14322" type="x-p"/>

entries.f67664f119e1cdd73386a90c202fa3a9a28d405a: <div eID="gen6033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Jehoshaphat’s Reign - 2 Chronicles 17-20</title> <div sID="gen6034" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat laboured to strengthen the kingdom both within and without. Not only did he place soldiers in the fenced cities, and removed the high places and the Astartes, but sought also to diffuse the knowledge of the law among the people, and by building castles and the possession of a well-equipped army, firmly to establish his power (2 Chron 17). In the course of years he married into the family of Ahab king of Israel, and, while on a visit in Samaria, allowed himself to be persuaded by Ahab to enter upon a joint war against the Syrians at Ramoth in Gilead, in which he all but lost his life, while King Ahab was mortally wounded in the battle (2 Chron 18). Censured on his return to Jerusalem by the prophet Jehu for this alliance with the godless Ahab, he sought still more earnestly to lead back his people to Jahve, the God of their fathers, bestirring himself to bring the administration of justice into a form in accordance with the law of God, and establishing a supreme tribunal in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.1-2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:1-11</reference>). Thereafter, when the Moabites and Ammonites, with the Edomites and other desert tribes, made an inroad into Judah, the Lord gave him a wonderful victory over these enemies. At a later time he yet again allied himself with the Israelitish king Ahaziah for the restoration of the commerce with Ophir; but the ships built for this purpose were broken in the harbour, so that the voyage was abandoned (2 Chron 20). Of all these enterprises of Jehoshaphat, none are mentioned in the book of Kings except the campaign entered upon with Ahab against Ramoth in Gilead, which is found in the history of Ahab, 1 Kings 22:2-35. Jehoshaphat’s reign itself is only characterized generally, but in such a way as to agree with the account in the Chronicle; and, in conclusion, the alliance with Ahaz for the purpose of making the voyage to Ophir is shortly narrated in 1Ki 22:41-53, but in a form which differs considerably from that in which it is communicated in the Chronicle. <div eID="gen6034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6035" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1">2Ch 17:1</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat’s efforts to strengthen the kingdom, internally and externally</hi>. - <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.1">2Ch 17:1</reference>, or rather the first half of this verse, belongs properly to the preceding chapter, since, when the son immediately follows the father on the throne, the successor is mentioned immediately: cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.31">2Ch 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.16">2Ch 12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.27">2Ch 24:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.9">2Ch 27:9</reference>, etc. Here, however, the account of the accession to the throne is combined with a general remark on the reign of the successor, and therefore it is placed at the commencement of the account of the reign; while in the case of Asa (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>) both come in immediately at the conclusion of the reign of his predecessor. Asa had shown himself weak against Israel, as he had sought help against Baasha’s attack from the Syrians (2Ch 16:1.), but it was otherwise with Jehoshaphat. He indeed put the fenced cities of his kingdom in a thoroughly good condition for defence, to protect his kingdom against hostile attacks from without (v. 20: but he walked at the same time in the ways of the Lord, so that the Lord made his kingdom strong and mighty (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.3-2Chr.17.5">2Ch 17:3-5</reference>). This general characterization of his reign is in <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Ch 17:6</reference> illustrated by facts: first by the communication of what Jehoshaphat did for the inner spiritual strengthening of the kingdom, by raising the standard of religion and morals among the people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6-2Chr.17.11">2Ch 17:6-11</reference>), and then by what he did for the external increase of his power (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12-2Chr.17.19">2Ch 17:12-19</reference>).
entries.8b517f16e2317ac74a646990a55fdf8990e30f3f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.2-2Chr.17.4">2Ch 17:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen6035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> He placed forces (חיל) in all the fenced cities of Judah, and garrisons (נציבים, military posts; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.16">1Ch 11:16</reference>) in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim, which is father Asa had taken; cf. 2Ch 15:8. God blessed these undertakings. Jahve was with him, because he walked in the ways of David his ancestor, the former ways, and sought not the Baals. The <hi type="italic">former</hi> ways of David are his ways in the earlier years of his reign, in contrast to the later years, in which his adultery with Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11) and the sin of numbering the people (1 Chron 21) fall. הבּעלים are all false gods, in contrast to Jahve, the one God of Israel; and here the word designates not only the Baal-worship properly so called, but also the worship of Jahve by means of images, by which Jahve is brought down to the level of the Baals; cf. Jdg 2:11. The ל before בּעלים stands, according to the later usage, as a sign of the accusative. In the last clause of <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.4">2Ch 17:4</reference>, “and not after the doings of Israel” (of the ten tribes), הלך, “he walked,” is to be repeated. The doing of Israel is the worship of Jahve through the images of the golden calves, which the author of the Chronicle includes in the לבּעלים דּרשׁ.
entries.fec17ee405f90707d5fdb7fb61bc9619fc6ab34f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">2Ch 17:5</reference> <div eID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6037" type="x-p"/> Therefore Jahve established the kingdom in his hand, i.e., under his rule; cf. 2Ki 14:5. All Judah brought him presents. מנחה, often used of tribute of subject peoples, e.g., in <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.11">2Ch 17:11</reference> of the Philistines, cannot here have that signification; nor can it denote the regular imposts of subjects, for these are not called מנחה; but must denote voluntary gifts which his subjects brought him as a token of their reverence and love. The last clause, “and there was to him (he attained) riches and honour in abundance,” which is repeated <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference>, recalls <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.28">1Ch 29:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.12">2Ch 1:12</reference>, and signifies that Jehoshaphat, like his ancestors David and Solomon, was blessed for walking in the pious ways of these his forefathers.
entries.5982bb3efe57e2016ff3745fe171277ef106cb35: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Ch 17:6</reference> <div eID="gen6037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6038" type="x-p"/> This blessing encouraged Jehoshaphat to extirpate from the land all idolatrous worship, and to teach the people the law of the Lord. לב נּבהּ, usually <hi type="italic">sensu malo</hi>, to be haughty, proud, cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.16">2Ch 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">2Ch 32:25</reference>; here <hi type="italic">sensu bono</hi>, of rising courage to advance in ways pleasing to God: and he removed the high places also, etc. עוד points back to <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.3">2Ch 17:3</reference> : not only did he himself keep far from the Baals, but he removed, besides, all memorials of the Baal-worship from Judah. On בּמות and אשׁרים, see on 2Ch 14:2.
entries.f696b8ab8d121e39957021369b5ac30caae29e0d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7-2Chr.17.9">2Ch 17:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen6038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6039" type="x-p"/> In the third year of his reign he sent five princes, i.e., laymen of high position, with nine Levites and two priests, into the cities of Judah, with the book of the law, to teach the law everywhere to the people. בּן־חיל is <hi type="italic">nom. prop</hi>., like בּן־חסד,   1Ki 4:10, בּן־דּקר,   1Ki 4:9, and is not to be translated as an adjective, as in lxx and Syr., partly on account of the ל <hi type="italic">praef</hi>., and still more on account of the singular, for the plural חיל בּני must be used when it is in apposition to לשׂרי. Nothing further is known of the men named; the designation of them as שׂרים suggests the idea that they were heads of families or fathers'-houses. אדוניּה טוב, too (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.8">2Ch 17:8</reference>), is one name. The “book of the law of Jahve” is the Pentateuch, not merely a collection of Mosaic laws, since in Jehoshaphat’s time the Mosaic book of the law (the Pentateuch) had been long in existence. יהוּדה בּערי סבב signifies to go through the cities of Judah in different directions; baa`aam limeed, to teach among the people (not the people). The mission of these men is called by the older theologians a solemn <hi type="italic">ecclesiarum visitatio, quam Josaphat laudabili exemplo per universum regnum suum instituit,</hi> and they differ in opinion only as to the part played by the princes in it. Vitringa, <hi type="italic">de synagoga vet.</hi> p. 389, in agreement with Rashi, thinks that only the Levites and priests were deputed <hi type="italic">ut docerent;</hi> the princes, <hi type="italic">ut auctoritate imperioque suo populum erudiendum in officio continerent eumque de seria regis voluntate certiorem facerent;</hi> while others, e.g., Buddaeus, refer to <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.9">2Ch 17:9</reference>, <hi type="italic">ubi principes pariter ac Levitae populum docuisse dicuntur,</hi> or believe with Grotius, <hi type="italic">docere et explicare legem non tantum sacerdotum erat et Levitarum, sed omnium eruditorum</hi>. Both views contain elements of truth, and do not mutually exclude each other, but may be harmonized. We can hardly confine למּד to religious teaching. The Mosaic law contains a number of merely civil precepts, as to which laymen learned in the law might impart instruction; and consequently the teaching probably consisted not merely in making the people acquainted with the contents of the law, but at the same time of direction and guidance in keeping the law, and generally in restoring and confirming the authority of the law among the people. In connection with this there were many abuses and illegalities which had to be broken down and removed; so that in this respect the task of the commission sent round the country by Jehoshaphat may be compared to a church inspection, if only we understand thereby not an inspection of churches in the Christian sense of the words, but an inspection of the religious and moral life of the communities of Israel under the old covenant.
entries.976cb86fbc03406fd6a91cb779ea4c72cfe297e1: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10-2Chr.17.11">2Ch 17:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen6039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6040" type="x-p"/> This attempt of Jehoshaphat brought him this blessing, that the terror of Jahve fell upon all the surrounding kingdoms; and not only did none of the neighbouring peoples venture to make war upon him, but also various tribes did homage to him by presents. Ramb. has already so understood the connection of these verses (<hi type="italic">erat hoc praemium pietatis Josaphati, quod vicini satisque potentes hostes non auderent adversus ipsum hiscere</hi>); while Berth. fails to apprehend it, saying that Jehoshaphat had time to care for the instruction of his people, because at that time the neighbouring peoples did not venture to undertake war against Judah. The words “terror of Jahve,” cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.13">2Ch 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>, and “all the kingdoms of the lands,” cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2Ch 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.30">1Ch 29:30</reference>, are expressions peculiar to the author of the Chronicle, which show that by these remarks he is preparing the way for a transition to a more detailed portrayal of Jehoshaphat’s political power. מן־פּלשׁתּים is subject, מן partitive: some of the Philistines brought him presents (for מנחה see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">2Ch 17:5</reference>), “and silver a burden,” i.e., in great quantity. משּׂא does not signify tribute, <hi type="italic">vectigal argento</hi> (Vulg.), for the word has not that signification, but denotes burden, that which can be carried, as in משּׂא לאן,   2Ch 20:25. - ערביאים or ערביּים, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.7">2Ch 26:7</reference>, and more usually ערבים, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.1">2Ch 22:1</reference>, are Arabian nomadic tribes (Bedâwin), perhaps those whom Asa, after his victory over the Cushite Zerah, had brought under the kingdom of Judah, 2Ch 14:14. These paid their tribute in small cattle, rams, and he-goats. (תּישׁים, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.35">Gen 30:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.15">Gen 32:15</reference>; Pro 30:31.)
entries.c88118f19deb95f54d3ea60f52aac45ae601a307: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12">2Ch 17:12</reference> <hi type="italic">Description of Jehoshaphat’s power</hi>. - 2Ch 17:12. And Jehoshaphat became ever greater, sc. in power. The partic. הולך expresses the continuous advance in greatness, cf. Ew. §280, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, as the <hi type="italic">infin. absol</hi>. does elsewhere, e.g., Gen 8:3. למעלה עד as in 2Ch 16:12. - He built castles in Judah. בּירניּות, only here and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.4">2Ch 27:4</reference>, from בּירנית, derivative formed from בּירה by the Syriac termination נית-, fem. of  ן-: castle, fortress. On מסכּנות ערי cf. 2Ch 8:4.
entries.41b2ba9dc6261d8c7e3f241b9dddfc31f8dbfcf8: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.13">2Ch 17:13</reference> וגו רבּה וּמלעכה is rightly translated by Luther, “<hi type="italic">und hatte viel Vorraths</hi>” (and had much store). מלעכה denotes here, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.7-Exod.22.10">Exo 22:7-10</reference>, property, that which has been gained by work or business. The signification, much work, <hi type="italic">opera magna</hi> (Vulg., Cler., etc.), as also Bertheau’s translation, “the works for equipping and provisioning the fortresses,” correspond neither to the context nor to the parallel (synonymous) second member of the verse. The work and trouble necessary to equip the cities of Judah does not correspond to “the valiant warriors in Jerusalem;” the only parallel is the goods and property which were in these cities, the provision of victuals and war material there stored up.
entries.6e1a468c1898eba6675632ae78a7043072f6911d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.14-2Chr.17.16">2Ch 17:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen6040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6041" type="x-p"/> The men fit for war passed in review according to their fathers'-houses. The male population of Judah fell into three divisions, that of Benjamin into two. The prince Adnah held the first place among the generals, with 300,000 men of Judah. ידו על, at his hand, i.e., with and under him, Jehohanan had the command of 280,000 men, and Amasiah over 200,000. השׂר is a contraction for אלפים שׂר. For what special reason it is so honourably recorded of Amasiah that he had willingly offered himself to the Lord (cf. for התנדּב, Jdg 5:9) has not been communicated.
entries.a892442ccf503250a289e342896ab0cb4d3b492d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.17-2Chr.17.18">2Ch 17:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen6041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6042" type="x-p"/> The Benjamites fell into two detachments: archers with shields (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:40</reference>) 200,000 men, under the chief command of Eliada, and “equipped of the army,” i.e., not heavy armed (Berth.), but provided with the usual weapons, sword, spear, and shield (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.24">1Ch 12:24</reference>), 180,000 under the command of Jehozabad. According to this statement, Judah had 780,000 warriors capable of bearing arms. These numbers are clearly too large, and bear no proportion to the result of the numbering of the people capable of bearing arms under David, when there were in Judah only 500,000 or 470,000 men (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.5">1Ch 21:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.5">2Sa 24:5</reference>); yet the sums of the single divisions appear duly proportioned-a fact which renders it more difficult to believe that these exaggerated numbers are the result of orthographical errors.
entries.e7e7af94097a6a921123a5ff8bdd2c230c64a7c0: <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.19">2Ch 17:19</reference> <div eID="gen6042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6043" type="x-p"/> These were serving the king. אלּה refers not to the above-mentioned men capable of bearing arms, for sheereet is not used of service in war, but to the commanders whom he had placed in the fortified cities of all Judah, “in which probably bodies of the above-mentioned troops lay as garrisons” (Berth.).  <chapter eID="2Chr.17"/> <div eID="gen6043" type="x-p"/>

entries.57775ac14c23a7d32512b6aea457e49a3fe62da7:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="17" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XVII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>ANd <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Kin. 15. 24.</ns0:note> Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead, and strengthened himself against Israel <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Against the King and People of Israel, who had molested the Kingdom of Judah with Wars <ns0:hi>all the days of Asa</ns0:hi> after that Sin of his mentioned, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 16. 2, &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And he placed forces in all the senced cities of Judah, and set garisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim, which Asa his father had taken.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the first ways of his <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">O<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        <ns0:hi>of his fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, & David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> father David <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which David walked in before he fell into those horrid Sins of Murder and Adultery. Or, <ns0:hi>in the ways of David,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers</ns0:hi> first ways: For the beginning of Asa's Reign was Laudable, as we have seen, though he declined at last. For it seems more pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable that this Passage is a Ref<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ection upon Asa, whose last ways were much his worst, and of whose Repentance we have no Evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence, than upon David, who, though he fell dreadfully in the Matter of Uriah, yet did manifestly repent of it and return to his first and holy course of Life, in which also he continued until death; having this Character given him by the Holy Ghost after his death, that he <ns0:hi>did right</ns0:hi> in all things, saving that of Uriah, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 15. 5.</ns0:note>, and sought not unto Baalim.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 But sought to the LORD God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Their Worship of the Calves or other Idols.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ore the LORD stablished the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>

See 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 10. 27, 28. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 10. 25. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 32. 23.</ns0:note>, and he had riches and honour in abundance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And his heart <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>encouraged.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> was lift up <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Above all discouragements and difficulties and fears, by which mens Hearts use to be cast down: He was Valiant and Resolute for God and his Ways.</ns0:note> in the ways of the LORD: moreover, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 19. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

And though Asa had done this before, yet either he did not do it tho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />roughly; or the Jews (who were many of them mad upon their Idols) had secretly made new Ones in the latter part of his Reign when he grew more infirm in Body and more remiss in Gods cause.</ns0:note> out of Judah.</ns0:p>

As Judges or Justices of Peace teach or instruct the People in the Laws of the Land when they deliver their Charges upon the Bench, so did these Princes in the Kings Name admonish and require the People to observe and obey the Laws of God, which were the Mu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nicipal Laws of that Land: The particular Explication and Inforce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment whereof they left to the Levites and Priests here following, who were sent for this End, and accordingly <ns0:hi>taught the People,</ns0:hi> v. 9.</ns0:note> in the cities of Judah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And with them <ns0:hi>he sent</ns0:hi> Levites, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> Shema<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Also <ns0:hi>some</ns0:hi> of the Philistins <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Who had been Subjects to this Kingdom ever since Davids Time, but, it seems, had neglected this Duty in the Times of his Predecessors, but now were moved by their own Fears to perform it.</ns0:note> brought Jeho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shaphat presents, and tribute-silver; and the Ara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bians <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either because he had upon some just occasion waged War against them and subdued them; though the Particulars of it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e not described in Scripture<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or because, they voluntarily put them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves under his Protection, in Recompence whereof they sent him those Presents: Or onely as a free Acknowledgment of their Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spects to him.</ns0:note> brought him flocks, seven thousand and se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven hundred rams, and seven thousand and seven hundred he-goats.</ns0:p>
